title: Treehouse of Horror XXXIV — Meaning, Genes, And Nothing Else

The episode was directed by Rob Oliver, and written by Jeff Westbrook, Jessica Conrad and Dan Vebber, one writer per segment, featuring guest voices from Kelsey Grammer, Kylie Jenner and Matthew Friend.

scenes.narration: What looks like free choice in Treehouse of Horror XXXIV is older than choice itself. "Treehouse of Horror XXXIV" is the fifth episode of the thirty-fifth season of the American animated television series The Simpsons, and the 755th episode overall. The episode was directed by Rob Oliver, and written by Jeff Westbrook, Jessica Conrad and Dan Vebber, one writer per segment, featuring guest voices from Kelsey Grammer, Kylie Jenner and Matthew Friend.

Nobody designed the part of Treehouse of Horror XXXIV you experience — it was inherited. This episode's stories were primarily spoofs of the films Snowpiercer, The Silence of the Lambs, Seven and Outbreak. The episode received mixed reviews, with segments "Wild Barts Can't Be Token" and "Lout Break" receiving negative reviews from critics, while "Ei8ht" received positive reviews.

Every serious account of Treehouse of Horror XXXIV eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Mayor Quimby announces his decision to close an art museum and convert its art into non-fungible tokens (NFTs). After sneaking inside it, Homer inadvertently digitizes Bart into an NFT, trapped in Homer's phone.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Treehouse of Horror XXXIV — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. After telling Marge, she enters the blockchain to rescue Bart with the guidance of "enlightened intellects" Kylie Jenner, Rob Gronkowski and Jimmy Fallon. Marge's value increases as she unintentionally destroys an NFT, consequently teleporting to the following carriage with pricier NFTs.

The selfish-gene reading of Treehouse of Horror XXXIV makes it less romantic and far more precise. After Marge and Bart return to the museum with Jenner's key, it is revealed that Homer turned himself into an NFT during Burns' offer. The blockchain train, driven by FOMO, runs out of fuel, rendering the NFTs, including Homer, nearly worthless.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. In an alternative ending to the fifth season episode "Cape Feare" (1993), Lisa watched Sideshow Bob brutally murder Bart on a houseboat drifting from Terror Lake to Springfield. Thirty years later, in a parody of the David Fincher series Mindhunter, a traumatized Lisa has become a renowned criminal profiler.

The feeling that Treehouse of Horror XXXIV means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. She is called upon by Springfield Police Department Officer Nelson Muntz to help investigate a series of murders with messages of the victims' names followed by "was the first" scrawled in blood. Seeking help in a Hannibal Lecter-style riddle or anagram from an imprisoned Bob, he instead mocks the idea as a plot cliché and provokes her wrath by bragging in a crude limerick about the murder of Bart.

Nothing in Treehouse of Horror XXXIV was built for you — it was built for reproduction. At the sixth victim's funeral, Lisa realizes the murder victims were all firstborns and searches a slaughterhouse owned by Ana Gram. Nelson is killed in the slaughterhouse, while Lisa discovers a nearby room resembling her own childhood bedroom.

The psychology underneath Treehouse of Horror XXXIV is simpler and older than the story on top. To her horror, Lisa watches security footage that shows her as Nelson's killer. The police arrest her and, in the same cell, Lisa reveals to Bob her Fight Club-style split personality. "Professor Lisa" was an unaware accomplice and the prison guard who put them in the same cell is her sister Maggie in disguise.

Behind Treehouse of Horror XXXIV sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Revealing she planned the entire killing spree so she could avenge the murder of Bart, Lisa first plays a vinyl of the aria Bob sang before killing Bart, "He is an Englishman" from the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta H.M.S Pinafore, and then brutally murders Sideshow Bob. At the power plant, Homer is caught eating doughnuts by Waylon Smithers.

The nihilist does not deny Treehouse of Horror XXXIV — he only refuses to flatter it. While he is complaining about society's unfair rules, a doughnut falls off and rolls, collecting nuclear waste and the DNA of assorted lab animals, but Homer runs after and eats it anyway. In a parody of Outbreak, the donut infects Homer's DNA, creating a virus that transforms the infected into his personality and likeness and which is spread through belching.

What culture calls destiny in Treehouse of Horror XXXIV is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. The virus spreads through Springfield and turns everyone else into Homer (including Kang and Kodos). Frink wishes to extract Homer's DNA to develop a cure, but he refuses, as he likes that everyone is just like he is and enjoys the lack of strict rules.

The genes do not care about Treehouse of Horror XXXIV; they care about copies. Thinking he will change his mind, Frink displays an infected Marge, but Homer instead finds Marge even more beautiful than ever before. Horrified, Frink pleads with Homer about how much the world needs rules and intelligent people to enforce them.

Take away the meaning and Treehouse of Horror XXXIV still functions — that is the disturbing part. Accepting defeat, Frink decides to call in a nuclear strike to destroy Springfield and contain the virus, but at the last second Homer accidentally tears Frink's suit and turns him into yet another Homer. The virus spreads worldwide via belching, filling the entire planet with a chorus of Homers singing "Just Like Paradise" by David Lee Roth.

The unconscious does not argue with Treehouse of Horror XXXIV; it simply acts first. The episode was directed by Rob Oliver and its showrunners were Matt Selman and Brian Kelley. Jeff Westbrook, Jessica Conrad, and Dan Vebber wrote "Wild Barts Can't Be Token", "Ei8ht", and "Lout Break", respectively.

Treehouse of Horror XXXIV feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Kylie Jenner as herself and Matthew Friend as Jimmy Fallon make up the guest voice cast. Kelsey Grammer appears as Sideshow Bob for the first time in four years since the season 31 episode "Bobby, It's Cold Outside".

The bleak reading of Treehouse of Horror XXXIV is also the most testable one. According to a Paste interview with Kelley, the ideas for "Ei8ht" and "Lout Break" were determined by the writers. Kelley and his team approached the first segment with the perspective that NFTs are not well understood, despite the hype surrounding them.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Treehouse of Horror XXXIV. Selman pointed out the contrast between the blockchain's popularity among celebrities and their lack of familiarity with it. Selman described Jenner's willingness to make fun of herself as contributing to the "comedic integrity".

The self that experiences Treehouse of Horror XXXIV is a committee, not a king. In creating "Ei8ht", Kelley directed Grammer with significant ease, saying that Grammer "just knows" Sideshow Bob. Its story was based on an episode idea involving a future Sideshow Bob.

Reproduction explains more of Treehouse of Horror XXXIV than any philosophy dares to admit. Kelley said that Vebber had had a plan for a pandemic episode that changed during the COVID-19 pandemic; it was the basis for the last segment, in which they made a "fun" concept that could let the actors "stretch a little". Due to the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike, the team had to rewrite the script months before what was planned, but only part of the animation was finished before the strike.

Once you see Treehouse of Horror XXXIV as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Chung landed the episode during the strike, Kelley approved them as "the reason the episode works". The related 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike did not influence the production of season 35 as the SAG-AFTRA contract did not affect The Simpsons.

The story Treehouse of Horror XXXIV tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. The plot of "Wild Barts Can't Be Token" references the 2013 film Snowpiercer. The title is a pun on the 1991 film Wild Hearts Can't Be Broken.

Meaning is not found in Treehouse of Horror XXXIV — it is manufactured for it. "Ei8ht" references the 1991 film The Silence of the Lambs and the likeness of films directed by David Fincher, including Seven (1995), stylized as Se7en. Writing for Bubbleblabber, critic Daniel Kurland gave the episode a 5.5 out of 10.

The cold light on Treehouse of Horror XXXIV leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. He felt that the episode was too fast-paced and took as examples the lack of an opening sequence and of a clear explanation for Homer digitizing Bart in "Wild Barts Can't Be Token". Kurland said that Treehouse of Horror series already has a recurring "'multiple Homer' concept", therefore making "Lout Break" overdone.

Treehouse of Horror XXXIV did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Hindustan Times's Tuhin Das Mahapatra opined that the episode's approach to contemporary topics like NFTs felt outdated. Das Mahapatra considered "Ei8ht"'s plot as being more sinister and exciting and a "welcome change of tone" from the first segment, while also enjoying the humorous nature of "Lout Break".

The honest version of Treehouse of Horror XXXIV starts by giving up the comforting part. In his conclusion, he mentioned criticism that the episode's references felt "out of place" and that it was an example of The Simpsons' social commentary becoming less clever. For The Salt Lake Tribune critic Scott Pierce, the episode was a "major disappointment".

Strip Treehouse of Horror XXXIV of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Pierce stated that the first segment was boring and the train would only make sense to viewers of Snowpiercer or its television adaptation. Sideshow Bob's return did not contribute to his enjoyment of the episode.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Treehouse of Horror XXXIV shows exactly where that breaks. In his opinion, "Lout Break" was "neither scary nor funny" and the Outbreak reference felt outdated.
